name: Non-syndromic Rectal Atresia

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical and Radiological Diagnostic Criteria for Rectal Atresia

criteria.description: Absence or imperforate anal opening on physical examination
Evidence of distal bowel obstruction with abdominal distension and failure to pass meconium
Radiological imaging (contrast enema or distal colostogram) demonstrating rectal discontinuity or atresia
No clinical or genetic evidence of syndromic associations or other congenital anomalies

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of absent anal opening, clinical signs of distal bowel obstruction, and radiologic confirmation of rectal discontinuity without syndromic features
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is primarily clinical supported by imaging; genetic testing is not routinely indicated unless syndromic features are suspected.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Imperforate anus with absent anal opening
Complete rectal discontinuity confirmed by imaging

common.symptomName: Abdominal distension due to distal bowel obstruction
searchTerms: abdominal swelling due to bowel obstruction

common.symptomName: Failure to pass meconium within 24-48 hours after birth
searchTerms: no stool passed within first two days
failure to pass first bowel movement

common.symptomName: Visible perineal dimple or fistula absent
searchTerms: no visible skin dimple near anus

occasional.symptomName: Constipation in early infancy (if partial obstruction present)
Urinary tract infection secondary to associated anomalies
searchTerms: kidney infection due to associated problems

rare.symptomName: Associated sacral anomalies detected on imaging
searchTerms: lower spine defects seen on imaging

rare.symptomName: Neonatal sepsis secondary to bowel perforation
searchTerms: newborn blood infection from bowel leak
infection in baby from bowel rupture

laboratory: Normal routine blood tests unless complications present
Possible leukocytosis if infection or sepsis develops
imaging: Contrast distal colostogram showing rectal discontinuity
Abdominal X-ray demonstrating dilated proximal bowel loops
Ultrasound to exclude associated renal or sacral anomalies
genetic: No known consistent genetic mutations in isolated non-syndromic cases
Genetic testing reserved for suspected syndromic cases
other: Physical examination revealing imperforate anus without fistula
Absence of associated congenital anomalies differentiates from syndromic forms

distinguishingFeatures: Presence of fistulous tract to perineum or urogenital tract
Often associated with other congenital anomalies
Delayed passage of meconium with chronic constipation

redFlags: Failure to pass meconium within 48 hours after birth
Signs of bowel perforation or sepsis
references: Levitt MA, Peña A. Anorectal malformations. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2007;2:33.
Holschneider AM, Hutson JM. Anorectal Malformations in Children: Embryology, Diagnosis, Surgical Treatment, Follow-up. Springer; 2006.
